title: Most Training Builds Skills. The Best Builds Networks.
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that organizational connection is a matter of design rather than personality, and that most training deliberately or accidentally works against it. Citing Rob Cross on informal networks and Amy Edmondson on psychological safety, she shows how departmental budgets, function-based promotion and siloed training keep people in single lanes with tunnel vision. Her alternative is to build connection into onboarding rotations, cohort-based programs that solve real organizational problems, and the way high performers are evaluated. She positions Learning and Development as the function best placed to architect these network moments, shifting its question from whether people learned to whether the organization became better at collaborating and adapting. She admits bandwidth is a real obstacle and that she has no perfect answer.
points: Connection is structural, so telling people to collaborate more or running team-building exercises will not fix weak networks without systems that make connection natural.
Rotating new hires through functions during onboarding is messier at first but gives them the map of who to call and how their work fits together.
Cohort learning that mixes departments and works on real organizational problems turns a program into a network moment and builds trust.
L&D is uniquely placed to see across silos and should act as a curator of connection rather than of content.

Performance reviews should ask who people collaborate with beyond their team and whom they have helped succeed, since technical high performers who bring no one along replicate isolation when promoted.
quotes: Connection gets treated as little more than a personality trait—something for people with emotional intelligence—and a nice-to-have. But this overlooks an important reality about the role of connection in organizational success: it’s rooted not in personality, but in design.

Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety and teaming supports this, too. People are more likely to reach across boundaries, ask for help, and share knowledge when they have existing relationships and understand the context of others’ work.

Cross’s research shows that the highest-performing organizations deliberately design structured opportunities for people to connect across boundaries in what he calls “network moments.” Fortunately for us, learning programs, when curated with care and intention, can be exactly that.

When L&D designs a learning program, it’s not just about deciding what content to create and deliver; it’s about deciding who comes together in the same room, what problems they work on, how they interact, and which relationships have the ability to form where they might not otherwise. In this context, every connection is an opportunity to create a “network moment” that helps solve a problem.

Instead of asking whether people learned something, we should be asking about whether an initiative strengthened our ability to collaborate, adapt, and solve problems. Simply put, however, this is a the difference between focusing on individual performance and organizational performance.

I also know that you can’t fix weak networks simply by telling people to “collaborate more” or by hosting a few team-building exercises. You fix weak networks by designing systems that make connection natural.
